explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Verse 12 says Eli's sons were wicked men with no regard for the LORD, and verse 13 says they had no regard for the custom of the priests with the people either. So the custom was there. They just didn't care about it. It's like a recipe taped to the oven that somebody keeps ignoring.

That's right, friend. Eli, the priest at Shiloh, had two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, and the text says they were wicked men who had no regard for the LORD or for the custom of the priests with the people (1 Samuel 2:12-13). The custom was real, and they walked right past it. I've seen a cookie sheet get more respect than that.

Yes, a three-pronged meat fork. Verse 13 says the servant of the priest comes with it while the meat is boiling. Three prongs means three chances to grab something. Picture a guy showing up to your cookout with his own personal harpoon.

Close to the neighborhood, friend, but no basin here. Verse 13 says the servant comes with a three-pronged meat fork. The pans, kettles and pots are what the fork gets stuck into. A basin would at least be something you could hand back.

I get why a knife comes to mind, but the text doesn't mention one. Verse 13 says the servant of the priest comes with a three-pronged meat fork. Three prongs, not one blade. Whatever that fork pulls up out of the pot is what he's after.

Himself. Verse 14 says the priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. No sharing, no asking, just whatever came up on the prongs. That's a guy who treats the whole potluck like his personal buffet.

Good thought, since it was a sacrifice, but that's not what verse 14 says. The priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. The fork went in the pot and the meat went to him. The altar never got a turn.

That would've been a kind ending, friend, but the text doesn't go that way. Verse 14 says the priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. The poor aren't in this verse at all. It all went to the priest.

Not just a few, friend. Verse 14 says, “This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.” That word all matters. Nobody got skipped. Imagine every single person in line getting the same fork treatment.

That's right. Verse 14 says, “This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.” Not some of them, not the unlucky ones, all of them. If you came to Shiloh with a sacrifice, you were in the fork's path.

Raw. The servant tells the man to give the priest meat to roast, because the priest “will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw” (1 Samuel 2:15). So the man's sacrifice is still being prepared and the servant is already placing an order. That's like walking into my bakery and asking for the dough before I've even turned on the oven.

Salted is a fair guess, friend, but salt never comes up. In verse 15 the servant says the priest “will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw.” The meat is for roasting, and the priest wants it raw. He's not even interested in the version that's being cooked right there.

Dried isn't what the text says. The servant tells the man that the priest “will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw” (1 Samuel 2:15). He wants it raw so he can roast it himself. A picky customer, and not even a paying one.

explanations.answer: Give it now or I take it by force
explanations.explanation: Yes. The servant says, “No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!” (1 Samuel 2:16). The man asked for the fat to be burned first, and that was the whole request. He got a threat in return, which is a rough way to end a conversation.

explanations.answer: Fine but the priest wants extra
explanations.explanation: That would've been a little polite for this servant, friend. He doesn't give in at all. He says, “No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!” (1 Samuel 2:16). No deal and no extra, just a demand.

explanations.answer: Then the priest will take none
explanations.explanation: If only. The servant doesn't back off one inch. Verse 16 has him say, “No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!” The man asked him to wait, and the servant answered with a threat.

True. Verse 17 says, “…the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD…” Severe is a strong word, and the text picked it. Whatever anybody else made of the fork and the threats, the LORD saw it as a serious matter.
Not this time, friend. Verse 17 says, “…the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD…” The text uses the word severe, plain and clear. It's not a small thing to the LORD.

Contempt. Verse 17 says, “…they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt.” That offering belonged to the LORD, and these young men handled it like leftovers. Contempt means looking down on something, and that's how the text describes it.

I wish that were it, friend, but care is the opposite. Verse 17 says, “…they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt.” Care would have meant waiting for the fat to burn. Contempt means they grabbed what they wanted.

Fear would've changed this whole story. The text says the opposite in verse 17: “…they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt.” Eli's sons had no regard for the LORD (1 Samuel 2:12), so fear wasn't slowing them down. Contempt is the word the text gives.

A little robe. Verse 19 says his mother would make him a little robe each year and bring it to him. Hannah, Samuel's mother, sews it herself. Every year, a fresh one, which tells me somebody keeps growing.

A belt would be handy, but it's not in the text. Verse 19 says Hannah, Samuel's mother, would make him a little robe each year. She made it and she brought it. A robe is the one thing the verse names.

Sandals would've been a nice gift, friend, but the text says something else. Verse 19 says Hannah, Samuel's mother, would make him a little robe and bring it to him each year. She made it by hand. Nothing in the verse mentions anything for his feet.

Three sons and two daughters. Verse 21 says the LORD attended to Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. That's five more children, on top of Samuel. A full table, and I bet a loud one.

That's a lovely number, friend, but the text gives a bigger one. Verse 21 says Hannah gave birth to three sons and two daughters. The LORD attended to her, and the house got a lot fuller. Five children is quite the batch.

Close on the count of sons, but not the right mix. Verse 21 says the LORD attended to Hannah, and she gave birth to three sons and two daughters. So there were daughters, and five children altogether. The numbers matter here, so I'm glad you're checking.

Not this time, friend. Eli says the opposite: “…it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people.” He's heard what people are saying about his sons, and he's not happy about it. That's a hard thing for a father to say to his own sons.

That's right. Eli says to his sons, “No, my sons; it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people.” He says he hears about their wicked deeds from all these people (1 Samuel 2:23). People were talking, and it wasn't a compliment.

explanations.answer: No one can step in for him
explanations.explanation: That's the question hanging in the air. Eli says, “If a man sins against another man, God can intercede for him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” (1 Samuel 2:25). He asks it as a question, and he leaves it right there. I think he wants his sons to feel how big that is.

explanations.answer: Only Eli can step in for him
explanations.explanation: Eli doesn't put himself in that spot, friend. He asks, “…if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” (1 Samuel 2:25). His question points to nobody being there to step in. He doesn't say he can do it.

explanations.answer: His family can step in for him
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thought, but Eli doesn't say it. In verse 25 he asks, “…if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” He doesn't answer with family, or anyone else. The question is left hanging, and it's meant to make his sons stop and think.

Not here, friend. Verse 25 says, “But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death.” Eli warned them, and they kept going. It's a heavy verse, and the text doesn't soften it.

That's right. The text says, “But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death.” (1 Samuel 2:25). Eli spoke up, and his sons didn't take it in. It's a heavy moment, and I won't joke about it.

explanations.answer: In favor with the LORD and with man
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 26 says, “And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man.” Right next to all that trouble with Eli's sons, Samuel is growing. It's a bright spot in a dark chapter.

explanations.answer: In honor among the city elders
explanations.explanation: That sounds official, friend, but the elders aren't in this verse. Verse 26 says Samuel “continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man.” Favor with the LORD and with man is the one the text gives. I'd take that over a fancy title any day.

explanations.answer: In charge of the priests' servants
explanations.explanation: Given what those servants were up to, I'm glad that's not the answer. Verse 26 says the boy Samuel “continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man.” Being in charge of anyone isn't mentioned. He's just growing up, and the LORD and the people are pleased.

Priest. In verse 28 the LORD says, “…out of all the tribes of Israel I selected your father to be My priest…” He picked Eli's father out of every tribe, so it was a big honor. That makes what happens next even harder to hear.

That's a good job, friend, but not the one in the verse. The LORD says He selected Eli's father “to be My priest, to offer sacrifices on My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod in My presence” (1 Samuel 2:28). He was picked for the priesthood. The priests were the ones working at the altar.

No crown in this verse. In verse 28 the LORD says He selected Eli's father out of all the tribes of Israel to be His priest. That means offering sacrifices, burning incense and wearing an ephod. Priest is the job the text names.
Sons. The LORD tells Eli, “You have honored your sons more than Me…” (1 Samuel 2:29). That's a hard thing for a father to hear, and the text doesn't blur it. Eli's sons were the ones he put first.
Elders aren't in this verse, friend. The LORD tells Eli, “You have honored your sons more than Me…” (1 Samuel 2:29). It's about Eli's own family, up close. That's why it lands so hard.

The servants did plenty of grabbing, but they're not who the LORD names here. He tells Eli, “You have honored your sons more than Me…” (1 Samuel 2:29). The word is sons. It's personal, and it's meant to be.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “For I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained.” (1 Samuel 2:30). Disdained is a different word than overlooked. It's a small word swap, but it changes the whole verse.

That's right. The LORD says, “For I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained.” (1 Samuel 2:30). The first half matches, but disdained isn't the same as overlooked. Two groups, two very different outcomes.

explanations.answer: They will both die on the same day
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “They will both die on the same day.” (1 Samuel 2:34). Hophni and Phinehas are Eli's two sons, the priests at Shiloh, and this is the sign He gives Eli. I think this one hurts, so I'll just say it plainly and move on.

explanations.answer: They will be taken captive together
explanations.explanation: The sign is heavier than that, friend. The LORD says of Hophni and Phinehas, Eli's two sons, “They will both die on the same day.” (1 Samuel 2:34). Captivity isn't in this verse. It's a hard word, and the text means it.

explanations.answer: They will die many years apart
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. The LORD tells Eli about his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, “They will both die on the same day.” (1 Samuel 2:34). The sign is that it happens together, on one day. I think this is one of the heavy parts, and it's okay to feel that.

True. The LORD says, “He will do whatever is in My heart and mind.” (1 Samuel 2:35). After all that trouble with Eli's sons, this priest is described very differently. He's called faithful, and that word carries the whole verse.

Not false, friend. In verse 35 the LORD says of the faithful priest, “He will do whatever is in My heart and mind.” It's right there in the text. After a chapter of priests who didn't, that's a welcome change.

Priestly. Verse 36 has them pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.” They used to grab the best of the meat, and now they're asking for bread. What a turnaround.

Fancy guess, friend, but nobody's asking for a crown. Verse 36 has them pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.” They're asking for a priestly office. That's the family business they're trying to get back into.

No soldiers in this verse. The people left in Eli's house plead, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.” (1 Samuel 2:36). Priestly is the word. It's a long way from where Eli's sons started.
